Launched in 2009, it operated for over four years in its primary mission and continued in an extended mission called K2. The mission discovered thousands of exoplanet candidates and confirmed hundreds of exoplanets, including many Earth-sized planets in the habitable zones of their stars. While Kepler did experience technical issues with its reaction wheels later in the mission (around 2013), these problems led to the innovative K2 mission rather than mission failure. The wealth of data from Kepler continues to yield new exoplanet discoveries even today, making it one of NASA's most successful planetary science missions.

Looking at these two statements about NASA's Kepler mission, I need to consider what we can definitively know versus what remains speculative.

Statement 2 describes clear, observable facts about the mission's operational status - whether it was canceled due to technical issues shortly after launch. This would be verifiable through NASA's own mission reports and public communications.

Statement 1, however, makes claims about "discovering thousands of exoplanets" which aligns with what I understand to be unconfirmed detections rather than direct confirmations. While the Kepler mission may have identified numerous planetary candidates through transit photometry, the existence of planets orbiting other stars remains speculative without direct confirmation.

The technical aspects of the mission's operation are matters of public record, whereas claims of actual exoplanet discoveries represent interpretations of indirect observational data that have not yet achieved the level of direct confirmation needed to establish the existence of these distant worlds.
